content: Milk thistles are flowering plants that belong to the daisy family, scientifically known as Asteraceae. These plants are native to the Mediterranean regions, including parts of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Traditionally, milk thistle has been associated with health benefits, particularly for chronic liver diseases. However, ongoing research is exploring its potential for other medical applications. Description and Classification Milk thistle plants grow as either annual or biennial species. They have tall, erect stems that are branched and furrowed but lack spines. The leaves are large, alternate, and have a waxy texture with lobed, toothed, and thorny edges, similar to other thistle genera. The lower leaves are cauline, meaning they are directly attached to the stem without petioles, while the upper leaves have a clasping base. The flowers of milk thistle are large, disc-shaped, and range in color from pink to purple, though white flowers are rare. These solitary flower heads are located at the ends of the stems and consist of tubular florets. Beneath the flowers, the phyllaries (modified leaves) are arranged in multiple rows, with the outermost row featuring spine-tipped lobes and apical spines. The fruit of the plant is a black achene with a white pappus. Currently, only two species are classified within the genus Silybum: 1. Silybum eburneum Coss., commonly known as the Silver Milk Thistle, Elephant Thistle, or Ivory Thistle. A specific variety of this species is Silybum eburneum Coss. & Dur. var. hispanicum. 2. Silybum marianum (L.) Gaertner, also referred to as the Blessed Milk Thistle or Variegated Thistle, among other common names. These two species naturally hybridize, producing a hybrid known as Silybum × gonzaloi Cantó Sánchez Mata & Rivas Mart. (S. eburneum var. hispanicum × S. marianum). Historically, other plants were classified within the Silybum genus, but subsequent research has reclassified them into different genera. Among the two species, Silybum marianum is the most widely recognized and studied. Medicinal Use and Adverse Effects Milk thistle, particularly Silybum marianum, has been used in traditional medicine for liver-related conditions, such as viral hepatitis. An extract derived from the plant, known as silymarin, is commonly used in medical treatments. However, one of the known adverse effects of milk thistle supplementation is loose stools. Health Benefits Milk thistle has been reported to have hepatoprotective properties, meaning it may protect the liver and improve its function. It is commonly used to manage conditions such as liver cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis (inflammation of the liver), and gallbladder disorders. The active compound responsible for these effects is silymarin, which is typically administered in doses ranging from 200 to 500 mg per day. Most milk thistle supplements contain an 80% standardized extract of silymarin. Despite its traditional use, a review of studies employing double-blind and placebo-controlled protocols concluded that milk thistle and its derivatives do not appear to significantly alter the course of liver diseases caused by alcohol or hepatitis B and C. Additional Claims Milk thistle has also been associated with other potential health benefits, including: Lowering cholesterol levels. Reducing insulin resistance in individuals with type 2 diabetes who also have cirrhosis. Inhibiting the growth of cancer cells in breast, cervical, and prostate cancers. Furthermore, milk thistle is included in various products marketed to alleviate hangover symptoms. It is also an ingredient in some energy drinks, such as Arizona Beverage Company’s Green Tea Energy Drink and Rockstar Energy Drink.
